extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying equitable remedies and trial practice in patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and procedural standards governing applications for, and defenses to, equity injunctions in patent infringement matters, and the division of questions of law and fact (especially novelty/identity) between court and jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use prior to grant as a defence in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a good defence, that, prior to the granting of the patent, the inventor had allowed the invention to go into public use, without objection; but that it should be clearly established by proof, that such public use was with the knowledge and consent of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Wyeth v. Stone. The text notes this is the same as one of the statute defences in an action at law and may be made in equity. Emphasizes requirement of clear proof of inventor's knowledge/consent to the public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will not aid a claimant who encouraged or acquiesced in infringement (laches)
rubrics_metrics.description: General principle of equity jurisprudence: the court will not lend its extraordinary aid to any claimant who has encouraged or acquiesced in an infringement of his right, or who has unreasonably delayed prosecuting for such violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in patent and copyright cases (cases cited: Lewis v. Chapman; Saunders v. Smith). If plaintiff knew of widespread disregard of his exclusive right and stood by, the court will dismiss bill on ground of laches or want of exclusive possession foundational to injunction relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay/laches may bar injunction but can be excused for difficulty obtaining evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a patentee must not lie by and induce others to incur risk, delay to institute proceedings may be explained by the difficulty of getting evidence of the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text acknowledges that what counts as reasonable delay depends on circumstances (cases cited). Courts consider reasons for delay; undue delay or delay for convenience can preclude equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence or conduct can amount to abandonment or surrender of patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If, for a series of years, the patentee acquiesces, without objection, in the known public use by others of his invention, such conduct will afford a very strong presumption of an actual abandonment or surrender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Justice Story: overt acts or express dedication can abandon rights; open encouragement or silent acquiescence that misleads defendants may be treated as surrender and bars equitable relief. Cases: Rundell v. Murray, Saunders v. Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must give public notice of any qualified allowance of public use
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee intends to surrender his exclusive right in a qualified manner or for a qualified trade, he should at the time give public notice of the nature and extent of his allowance of the public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without clear public notice, aquiescence in public use means the patentee no longer claims exclusivity for that use and cannot later seek injunction to restrain extension (example: Wyeth v. Stone discussion on domestic vs foreign trade).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of exclusive possession required for interim equitable protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of a patent for a certain length of time gives such a title as the court will protect until a trial at law can be had, but the court ought to have very satisfactory evidence of exclusive possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collard v. Allison: conflicting evidence among manufacturers about whether they abstained from making the product raises doubt and prevents interference by injunction. Courts require convincing evidence of exclusive possession to justify interim protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions in United States equity require notice and are special
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases of proceedings in equity to restrain the infringement of patents, in the courts of the United States, the injunction can, at no time, be applied for without notice to the adverse party, giving him an opportunity to oppose it; and, therefore, the injunction is always special.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes common and special injunctions. Practical consequence: motion practice will involve affidavits and opportunity to respond; provisional orders must be tailored to parties and issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits required on injunction application: must show title, infringement, and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the injunction is applied for before an answer has been filed, the plaintiff, in addition to the allegations in his bill, must read affidavits to show his title, and the fact of infringement, especially if the defendant appears and offers evidence against the one or the other; and, in strictness, these affidavits should cover the issue of the patent, the novelty of the invention, and all other facts necessary to the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the bill itself is sworn/verified and the defendant does not file affidavits denying title, practice may treat the bill as verification of title. But when the defendant attacks title, plaintiff must present auxiliary proof beyond the bill to make out prima facie right to injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: If defendant attacks title by affidavit after answer, plaintiff must produce auxiliary proof
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant attacks the title by affidavit, it must be supported by auxiliary proof in addition to the bill, in order to make out the prima facie right to an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit challenges to title invoke the need for additional supporting evidence; mere verification by the bill may be insufficient when defendant credibly disputes title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of plaintiff affidavits after answer is discretionary; courts may permit rebuttal proof
rubrics_metrics.description: There is authority both ways whether the plaintiff is at liberty to read affidavits in support of his title after an answer denying it; the better view is that the plaintiff may show from counter-evidence that the case is different from that disclosed by the defendant's answer and thus fortify his right to an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: Justice McLean held plaintiff not entitled in one circuit (Brooks v. Bicknell), Justice Woodbury allowed reading affidavits; Poor v. Carleton and other decisions support that granting/dissolving injunctions rests in court's discretion and affidavits may be read by plaintiff post-answer in cases of irreparable mischief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting or dissolving injunctions rests in the sound discretion of the court (irreparable harm principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole question of granting or dissolving injunctions, in cases of irreparable mischief, rests in the sound discretion of the court, after answer as well as before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court weighs affidavits and the balance of conveniences; even if an answer contradicts affidavits, the court may look into evidence on both sides sufficiently to determine probability of plaintiff establishing patent and grant or withhold injunction accordingly. Authorities: Poor v. Carleton; Orr v. Littlefield.

rubrics_metrics.name: On injunction motion, defendants must show plaintiff has no right or that defendants have a superior right
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendants must be prepared to make their entire defence either by showing from their answer or affidavits a want of right in the plaintiffs or a superior right in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plaintiff sets out rights and injuries by bill; law allows plaintiff rebutting evidence and generally precludes defendant from replying to such rebutting evidence by further proofs on his part in the immediate motion context. Rule 107 and practice notes cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between questions of law and questions of fact (novelty, identity, invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty, as generally employed, embraces invention and identity. Where there is no dispute as to identity or invention, the court may, without a jury, decide whether the invention as it stands has been made known to the public; but when identity or invention is disputed, the issues are matters of fact for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lang v. Gisborne: court held sale of copies amounted to publication in law when identity not disputed. If identity or invention is in dispute, jury should decide; court's role is to instruct on what constitutes novelty and sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication (sale/ circulation) effect on novelty can be a question of law when identity undisputed
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of a few copies unaccompanied by evidence of subsequent public user may amount to publication in law; whether that publication defeats novelty depends on the circumstances and extent of circulation — a single obscure copy differs from an encyclopaedia in general circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lang v. Gisborne and Stead v. Williams discussed. The degree of circulation and whether publication was effectively to the public are factual circumstances but, where identity is not in issue, the court may treat the question as one of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/invention (whether the thing patented is substantially different) is ordinarily a jury question when facts disputed
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee was the inventor and whether the patented thing is substantially different from prior known things is, in general, a question for the decision of the jury; the court's province is to give proper instructions as to what constitutes novelty and sufficiency of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Whittemore v. Cutter, Lowell v. Lewis, Carver v. Braintree, etc. If evidence in pais (public use) is presented, jury weighs it under court instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of specifications and identity between patents may be judicial when facts undisputed (but authorities conflict)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant claims his act is under another patent or that the plaintiff's invention is contained in a patent granted to a third party, the court has been held in many cases to have the exclusive province to pronounce upon identity when the facts are not disputed; however, authorities have conflicted and later decisions (e.g., reversal of Exchequer Chamber in Betts v. Menzies) have recognized that when facts are disputed the matter may require different treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Bovill v. Pimm, Betts v. Menzies, Bush v. Fox, Hills v. Evans. The treatise records the historical conflict and ultimate reversal of the Exchequer Chamber decision, illustrating that judicial determination of identity is appropriate only where factual dispute is absent; otherwise, jury issues may be implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable relief withheld where there's doubt as to novelty or validity
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is so much doubt as to the novelty of what is claimed, and as to the validity of a patent for such a manufacture, the court may refrain from interfering by injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collard v. Allison: discrepancy of testimony about industry practice created sufficient doubt to prevent injunction. Courts will not grant extraordinary equitable relief where substantial doubt about title or novelty exists.
